label: Three Geometries, One Question
notes: This chapter spanning printed pages 3 to 16 opens the whole course with one sharp question: what survives when straightness becomes intrinsic to a surface rather than borrowed from the surrounding Euclidean space. Flat, spherical, and hyperbolic worlds answer it differently, and the triangle angle sum is our first measuring instrument.

label: Euclid and the Fifth Postulate
notes: Euclid's first four postulates feel inevitable, but the fifth, the parallel postulate, always read like a theorem waiting to be proved. For two thousand years geometers tried to derive it and failed. That stubborn failure, not any success, is what eventually cracked open spherical and hyperbolic geometry as honest alternatives.

label: The Parallel Postulate Restated
notes: Playfair's clean restatement says exactly one line through an outside point misses a given line. Phrasing it this way isolates the single assumption we can vary. Keep it and you stay Euclidean; allow zero such lines and you get the sphere; allow infinitely many and you fall into the hyperbolic plane.

label: Geodesics: Straightest Paths
notes: On a curved surface the word straight has to be redefined intrinsically. A geodesic is the path an ant walks without ever turning left or right, and equivalently the locally shortest route between nearby points. Great circles play this role on the sphere, so they are the true straight lines of spherical geometry.

label: The Sphere: No Parallels
notes: Any two distinct great circles must intersect, in fact at two antipodal points, so the sphere admits no parallel lines at all. This is the geometry of zero parallels. The familiar lines of latitude are not geodesics, which is exactly why airplanes fly curved-looking routes that are actually the straightest available.

label: Spherical Triangles Bulge Outward
notes: Build a triangle from three great-circle arcs and its angles overflow. A triangle with a vertex at the pole and two on the equator already shows three right angles summing to two hundred seventy degrees. The corners push outward because the surface itself curves away beneath them, a visible fingerprint of positive curvature.

label: Angular Excess Measures Area
notes: Harriot's beautiful result turns geometry into bookkeeping: cut the sphere into lunes, overlay the triangle, and the leftover angle, the excess beyond a flat triangle, equals the triangle's area on the unit sphere. Excess is not an error to discard. It is the curvature integrated over the region the triangle encloses.

label: The Hyperbolic Plane: Many Parallels
notes: The hyperbolic plane reverses the sphere. Through a point off a line run infinitely many non-intersecting lines, two of them limiting and asymptotic. Visualized as a saddle or a crinkly lettuce leaf, there is too much surface near every point, so geodesics splay apart instead of converging the way they do on a sphere.

label: Hyperbolic Triangles Pinch Inward
notes: In hyperbolic geometry triangle angles fall short of two right angles, and the larger the triangle the larger the deficit. An ideal triangle with vertices at infinity has all three angles equal to zero. The corners pinch inward because the saddle pulls surface away, the mirror image of the sphere's outward bulge.

label: Excess and Defect Side by Side
notes: Lining the three worlds up shows one continuous dial. Angle sum greater than a straight pair signals positive curvature, exactly a straight pair signals flatness, and less signals negative curvature. The deviation, signed, is the angular excess. Curvature is not exotic; it is the leftover angle a careful triangle hands you.

label: Intrinsic versus Extrinsic
notes: Bend a sheet of paper into a cylinder and you have changed its embedding in space but not a single distance measured along the surface, so its triangles still sum to a straight pair. Intrinsic geometry is what an inhabitant can detect without leaving the surface, and angular excess is its loudest signal.

label: Curvature as the Common Thread
notes: The chapter closes by naming what all three pictures share. A single number, the Gaussian curvature, is positive on the sphere, zero on the plane, and negative on the saddle, and it equals the angular excess per unit area. Everything later in the book, geodesics, transport, and forms, grows from this seed.
